transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-10
Time: 15:00 - 15:52 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Aisha (StratusAI CTO), Ben (ML Eng), Lina (SRE), Raj (Product)
Links shared: Redwood edgecases deck (link), long-context benchmarks spreadsheet (link), security one-pager (link)

Summary (auto): quick demo focused on edge cases: long context handling, high TPS load patterns, streaming backpressure and timeouts. Customer provided traffic profile and asked about tail latencies, quantization tradeoffs, and private deployment constraints. Agreed next steps and pilot kickoff timelines.

00:00 Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining. this is Jordan from Redwood, I'm the account lead. With me are Priya and Carlos on the SE side. how're you all doing?
00:12 Aisha: good thanks. we pulled the infra folks on our side cause we want to validate a few things about real traffic — long context use, we also have some streaming clients.
00:22 Ben: yeah we've got a profile where some requests carry 32k tokens of context, and during peak we hit 1.2k TPS for embeddings and about 400 TPS for gen, so tail latencies and backpressure are super important.
00:34 Priya: perfect. that's exactly what this session will walk through. we'll demo API behavior, Console for tracing, and Optimize recommendations for batching/kv-cache/quantization. We'll surface failure modes like streaming backpressure and timeouts and how Redwood mitigates them.
00:45 Raj: quick ask up front — we are evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private. if you can touch on breakpoints where dedicated is necessary that helps.
00:56 Carlos: absolutely, we'll flag thresholds. also we'll show fallback policies when capacity constrained.

02:15 Priya: starting with the API: here is a typical generation call, we show how to set model, max tokens, stream true and stream-chunk-size. when you have long context the KV cache size and kernel selection change, which impacts latency.
03:05 Ben: on the KV cache, are you doing automatic prefix caching for repeated system prompts? we have lots of repeated onboarding history across users.
03:15 Priya: yes, we do prefix caching automatically for identical prefixes, and you can opt-in to warm caches via the Console. note: if context changes frequently, cache hit drops so batching becomes more relevant.

05:00 Jordan: demo time — Priya will take over the console and we'll simulate a long-context 25k token chat and then spin up load. Priya?
05:10 Priya: ok sharing screen. Console -> Routes -> Live trace. here's a sample request showing 24.8k tokens input, streaming enabled. notice the kernel profile suggests fp16 quantized path due to model and sequence length.
05:38 Aisha: hmm that model path line says 'quant 8pl' on my screen, is that a typo?
05:43 Priya: yeah auto transcript butter — that's 8-bit quant path, sometimes the UI label truncates for long names. sorry.
06:02 Carlos: starting synthetic load: target 500 TPS gen, 1.1k TPS embed with a 10% long-context tail. we'll show what backpressure looks like in the stream client.
06:25 Ben: when backpressure happens do you drop connections or buffer? our clients are mobile so we need predictable behavior.
06:33 Priya: good question. by default we apply flow-control: we will signal upstream and apply partial buffering; if buffers exceed configured soft limits we return an explicit backpressure error so clients can retry with slower rate. for mobile we recommend short streaming checkpoints and client-side exponential backoff.

08:00 [timestamp: synthetic load ramping; audible keys in background]
08:12 Speaker 1: 08:12 oh uh there's a spike — we see tail latency to 2.4s for small requests and to 9.2s for the long-context requests.
08:26 Priya: yep that's expected as the KV cache warmup hasn't happened on that synthetic run. once caches warm the long-context tail drops significantly. We're showing live traces per shard — notice the request routed to a fallback model variant with lower seq-optimizations to keep latency under SLO.

10:00 Aisha: about fallback — do you degrade quality or do you serve a smaller model? we can't accept large hallucinations.
10:12 Carlos: we prefer model variants that are quantized but still same architecture; if you have strict quality SLAs we recommend a canary policy that prefers higher-quality machines and falls back only during emergencies. for most workloads we route to a compatible variant that preserves top-k sampling settings.

12:30 Ben: can we see the Console's tracing of streaming timeouts?
12:40 Priya: sure. here is trace for a streaming session that hit the soft buffer limit. you'll see periodic heartbeat chunks then final error code 408-stream-timeout. the trace shows partial tokens returned and the retry suggestions.
13:05 Raj: 408-stream-timeout — is that a Redwood-specific code or standard http? our stack expects standard 5xx/4xx codes.
13:14 Priya: it's HTTP 408 mapped with an internal subcode we emit in headers: X-Redwood-Error: stream_timeout. We also provide a detailed retry-after and recommended safe-RPS in headers.

15:00 Jordan: moving to Optimize — the optimizer makes batching and quantization recs based on your traffic profile. we'll show live how switching to grouped batching at the gateway reduces token cost 22% for this workload.
15:30 Priya: toggling from naive batch of 1 to continuous batching at 8 reduces compute spikes and amortizes KV loads. note though it increases median latency by ~30ms which most customers accept.
16:00 Ben: long context + batching — isn't there an interaction where batching increases memory usage due to KV duplication?
16:12 Carlos: yes. Optimize will surface memory pressure and suggest quantization and per-model max context fallbacks. we also recommend sharded KV across GPUs to avoid duplication.

18:20 [background: typing]
18:35 Aisha: security questions — we've got SOC2, ISO requirements and KMS/HSM for keys. if we go private, can we manage our own KMS, and how are audit logs exposed?
18:46 Jordan: for Private and Dedicated we support customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS or HSM) and we stream audit logs to your CloudWatch or S3 with optional encryption at rest. Console shows per-request audit id and SSO binds.
18:59 Lina: SSO — do you integrate with SAML and SCIM? we need automated provisioning.
19:05 Priya: yes SAML and SCIM supported; RBAC roles map to Console permissions. we'll share the SAML guide in the security packet.

21:10 Ben: about test harness — we want to run a pilot with our sample traffic. what's realistic pilot duration and what do you instrument?
21:22 Jordan: typical pilot is 1–2 weeks; we collect per-route latency, token consumption, tail-latency distribution, and error rates. we'll also run a stress test to your target TPS with a handful of failure scenarios — network partition, model OOM, and streaming client slow consumption.

23:45 Priya: demo: now I'll force backpressure scenario — starting a client that reads slowly to simulate mobile with small read windows. watch the streaming chunks and error surface.
24:00 [console noise] 
24:15 Ben: i see chunk delays and eventually the connection resets with 502 upstream-reset. is that coming from the gateway or the model runner?
24:24 Priya: upstream-reset usually means we closed the connection due to client slow consumption. the gateway enforces soft timeouts and then tears down to preserve node health. we return structured guidance in trace.

26:00 Aisha: what's the best practice for mobile streaming clients — checkpointing or polling?
26:10 Carlos: checkpointing at every N tokens and resuming using cursor tokens works well. For unreliable networks, we recommend short streaming windows with a fallback to full-response polling if stream fails.

28:30 Ben: on the topic of timeouts, do you support tail-latency SLAs and billing credits if SLOs missed?
28:38 Jordan: for Dedicated we can contract latency SLOs with credits. Hosted has best-effort SLOs and we publish historical percentiles. Private deployments can have negotiated terms based on infra specs.

30:00 Priya: quick note on model compilation — runtime picks kernels based on sequence length distribution. longer contexts may choose different attention kernels which increase latency; Optimize will recommend kernel-friendly tokenization and chunking to avoid pathological kernel switches.
30:25 Ben: any heuristics for chunking long context?
30:31 Priya: yes, we recommend semantic chunk boundaries and batching similar-length requests. also precompute embeddings for static sections to avoid re-encoding long stable context.

32:00 [pause, someone muted] 
32:18 Raj: regarding pricing — at what point does dedicated become cheaper for us? with ~1.2k TPS embedding and 400 gen TPS our rough estimate was X tokens per month.
32:30 Jordan: rough rule: when predictable sustained throughput leads to committed GPU utilization over 60–70% it's worth dedicated. we'll run the spreadsheet against your expected monthly token counts and give a point estimate.

34:00 Ben: can Redwood handle multi-region failover without losing in-flight streams?
34:10 Carlos: in-flight streams are tied to the serving region; our recommended pattern is client retry with idempotency keys. for session continuity we can persist partial output to cache and resume but it's not transparent for active TCP streams. we can demo a cross-region failover pattern in the pilot.

36:45 Aisha: any notable pitfalls customers hit with long context?
36:52 Priya: common ones: (1) unexpected kernel switches at varying seq lengths causing jitter, (2) cache fragmentation when context varies slightly across users, (3) client-side assumptions about streaming heartbeats. Optimize catches many of these and flags prompts to break or precompute.

38:10 Ben: about quantization — is there a quality regression report? we want to quantify delta.
38:20 Priya: Optimize produces evals against your test prompts and returns quality deltas. we run A/B comparisons and show per-prompt regressions. If regression exceeds threshold we won't recommend that quant profile.

40:00 [screen: example eval results]
40:12 Raj: nice, I like the per-prompt regression heatmap. can that integrate with our CI?
40:18 Carlos: yes, we can export results as JSON and webhook into your CI to block rollouts.

42:00 Priya: let's summarize failure modes we demoed: slow client -> stream backpressure -> gateway returns 408/502 patterns; long context -> kernel switch -> tail spikes; heavy TPS -> queueing/backpressure and fallback routing.
42:20 Aisha: that matches our concerns.

44:00 Jordan: Recap & next steps: we'll send the long-context benchmark spreadsheet and security docs. Priya will share tail-latency dashboard and Optimize recommendations. We propose pilot start next Tuesday, 2026-04-14, pending your infra prep.
44:18 Aisha: sounds good. please also include dedicated pricing comparison vs hosted for 6/12 month commits.
44:26 Jordan: will do. Lina, please share VPC contact details and we'll loop in our infra team.
44:34 Lina: will do.

46:00 Ben: one last nit — instrumentation granularity: can we get per-route token cost breakdown?
46:06 Priya: yes per-route token-level breakdown is available and you can tag routes for cost centers. we'll attach an example dashboard.

48:30 Raj: any other questions?
48:36 Aisha: none from me, thanks for covering the edge cases in depth.
48:42 Jordan: thanks all. we'll follow up with the packet and schedule.

51:00 [call ends, brief small talk and goodbyes]
